similar_scenes.name: Decadencia y glam-rock
similar_scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
similar_scenes.desc: El rock siempre tuvo un elemento de decadencia, amoralidad y obscenidad; entre los Cockettes (1968) y el Rocky Horror Picture Show (1974) se convierte en producto de masas. Gran Bretaña lo llama glam-rock: T.Rex lo inaugura y lo casa con el hard rock; David Bowie lo lleva a su cima comercial convirtiendo el marketing en arte (Ziggy Stardust, la trilogía berlinesa con Eno). En EE UU, Alice Cooper, Sparks, Iggy Pop y Lou Reed (Berlin, Metal Machine Music, New York). El glam y la decadencia preparan el punk: Mott The Hoople, Be Bop Deluxe, New York Dolls, Heartbreakers, Dictators, Modern Lovers de Jonathan Richman, Runaways.
similar_scenes.family: Punk, new wave, hardcore y noise

podcast.title: Decline from Charts (1976-1977)
podcast.body: Glam rock largely disappeared from the music charts by 1976-1977, coinciding with the rise of punk rock and disco. Despite its decline, the theatricality and exaggerated costuming it introduced became a permanent part of the rock canon. "Glam was all but gone from the charts by the time punk rock and disco came along in 1976 and 1977."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: 1970s British Movement
podcast.body: Glam rock was a prominent music movement in Britain during the 1970s, featuring artists such as Bowie, T-Rex, The Sweet, and Gary Glitter. Its flashy fashion spurred a "Ted revival" around 1974, as a counter-reaction to its style. "This was in large part a response to the glam rock of the era, Boi, T-Rex, the sweet, Gary Glitter, and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Tribes of Alt-Rock

podcast.title: American vs. British Glam
podcast.body: David Bowie distinguished British glam from American glam, noting that British glam rock struggled to impact Middle America to the same extent as artists like Alice Cooper and Kiss. He described American glam as "butch manly glam with lots of guillotines and fireworks, muscle and metal," lacking the sexual ambiguity of British acts, which was the "only way Ohio could accept lipstick on males." "British glam rock never made an impact on Middle America to any extent."

srcs.episode: Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s
Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s

podcast.title: Birth and Popularity
podcast.body: Glam rock emerged and became popular in the early 1970s, though its peak period was relatively short. British music critic Simon Reynolds, who grew up in early 70s England, perceived glam as synonymous with pop music. "Why was Glam rock born? Why was it so popular? If only for a short period of time."

srcs.episode: Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s
Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s

podcast.title: Brief but Global Impact
podcast.body: Glam rock's "moment in the sun" was short-lived, primarily from 1971 to 1975, and largely a UK phenomenon with only David Bowie and Roxy Music gaining significant traction in North America. However, its DNA of "extremism, flamboyance, and theatricality" has spread globally across rock and pop, continually reappearing in fashion and music trends. "Glam was not around for very long. We can terribly put its moment in the sun from 1971 to 1975."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Critical Disdain (1970s)
podcast.body: Many rock critics of the era disliked glam rock. Mike West, writing for the *Daily News Journal* and *Murphy's Pro Tennessee* in 1974, described glam's greatest attraction as its "decadence," with "veiled reference to bisexuality, violence and falloness." He criticized the lack of musical substance, vividly picturing a 17-year-old boy in six-inch plastic heels, black stockings, a gold lame jumpsuit, pink hair, and heavy makeup, suggesting only The Who and The Allman Brothers Band still made "music." "glam rocks greatest attraction lies in its decadence."

srcs.episode: Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s
Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s

podcast.title: Decline and Enduring Influence
podcast.body: Glam and glitter rock largely became "extinct" by 1977, but their influence persisted throughout the 1980s, 1990s, and continues to be seen today. "And while glam and glitter were pretty much extinct by 1977, its influence continued into the 80s, 90s and even today."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Defining Trend of Early 1970s
podcast.body: The early 1970s were recognized as the era of glam rock, a musical movement characterized by artists embracing elaborate makeup and flamboyant costumes. Bands like Kiss adopted these theatrical aesthetics as part of this widespread trend. "this was the age of glam rock."

srcs.episode: Ep. 47 - Dick Clark's Entertainment Empire
Ep. 47 - Dick Clark's Entertainment Empire

podcast.title: Definition and Aesthetic
podcast.body: Glam rock, or glitter rock as Americans called it, was defined less by a specific rock style and more by the theatricality of its live performances. It was characterized by men in sparkles, sequins, spandex, feather boas, and high heel boots, pushing the gender-bending flamboyance initiated by Little Richard to its limits. The visual aspect was observed for its own sake, aiming to shock with costumes and stage antics. "The thing that makes glam glam or glitter rock as many Americans called it is not so much the style of rock as it is that theatrix that deliver the rock in a live performance."

srcs.episode: Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s
Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s

podcast.title: Definition and Characteristics
podcast.body: Glam rock was a theatrical form of rock, a distinct musical sub-genre, and a significant movement in fashion, culture, and non-binary sexuality. It served as a bridge between 1960s rock and the developments of the 1970s and beyond. Predominantly a British phenomenon in the early 1970s, its influence (1971-1975) is still pervasive in rock worldwide, contributing to the existence of many important and long-lasting genres today. "Glam was rock at its most theatrical. Not only was it a sound, a proper musical sub-shin, but it was also a movement in fashion, the clothes, the hair, the makeup."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Geographical and Temporal Scope
podcast.body: Primarily a British phenomenon that emerged in the early 1970s, with its core influential period spanning from about 1971 to 1975. Despite its relatively short duration and regional focus, its influence spread globally. "Yes, this was a thing in the early 70s and yes, it was mostly a British thing."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Glittery, Flamboyant Look
podcast.body: Glam rock, as exemplified by artists like David Bowie (during his Ziggy Stardust years) and the New York Dolls, was a genre that prioritized a glittery, flamboyant aesthetic in the early 1970s. For these artists, the specific clothes and makeup chosen were as crucial to their identity and impact as the music itself. "over in England, glam rock, the glittery, flamboyant look favored by David Bowie and Ziggy Stardust years was as much about the right clothes and the right makeup as it was about music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Fashion

podcast.title: Global Reach
podcast.body: The glam movement was extensive, featuring artists not only in the United Kingdom but also in the United States and even Japan, demonstrating its widespread international appeal. "el movimiento de la Llan tuvo artistas por todo el mundo. Y fue mucho más extenso de lo que muchas veces parece."

srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: Golden Age Inauguration
podcast.body: T-Rex's *Electric Warrior* (1971) is widely considered the album that officially inaugurated the "golden age" of glam music. "el electric warrior es el álbum que inaugura oficialmente la etapa adorada de la música glam."

srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: Influence on New Romantics Fashion
podcast.body: Glam rock significantly influenced the fashion sense of the New Romantics scene in the UK. Their style blended the "anything goes attitude" of punk with elements from glam rock, combined with romantic period looks, resulting in an "over the top" aesthetic with makeup and wild hairstyles. "a sense of fashion that blended the anything goes attitude of punk with glam rock, with looks from the romantic period of England, hence the name New Romantics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 4: Alt-Dance

podcast.title: Influence on Suede
podcast.body: David Bowie's glam rock period of the early 1970s was a significant influence on Suede, particularly singer Brett Anderson. By 1992, this glam aesthetic felt fresh and fabulous again, contributing to Suede's unique style. "Singer Brett Anderson was a fan of David Bowie's glam rock period of the early 1970s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Influences and Complexity
podcast.body: Despite its perceived simplicity, glam music was more complex than often assumed, amalgamating numerous musical influences and movements from the UK during the 1960s. These included psychedelic music, folk, early pop-rock, and the flamboyant personalities of rock legends. "la música glamera mucho más compleja de lo que muchas veces parece."

srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: Introduction and Influence
podcast.body: Glam rock emerged in the late 1960s and early 1970s as a highly shocking and outrageous style, fundamentally altering rock music despite its relatively short lifespan of four to five years. Its influence is still observable and felt today. "This is the surprising history of glam rock. It still lives and can still make things very interesting."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: London Scene and Public Perception
podcast.body: Glam rock was a prominent musical and fashion movement in London. While it was immensely popular among "teeny-boppers," many perceived it as having the "trappings of disposable bubblegum pop," indicating a divide in its cultural reception. "While glam rock was all the rage among teeny-boppers and had the trappings of disposable bubblegum popped to many people, Bowie was ready to take things to the next level."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 2

podcast.title: Musical Characteristics
podcast.body: Glam rock was musically simpler and more spontaneous than the elaborate psychedelic and progressive rock of the late 1960s. Recordings were less polished, prioritizing spontaneity. Musically, it incorporated remnants of psychedelic guitar (distorted, eccentric), folk music influences (melancholic ballads), and the love for simple, catchy melodies from early pop-rock like The Beatles. "era musicalmente más sencillo, era muy espontáneo, las grabaciones no eran lo más pulido del mundo, primaba muchísimo lo que era la espontanidad."

srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: New Romantics' Nostalgia
podcast.body: The New Romantic movement, which emerged after the angry nihilism of punk, expressed a longing for the earlier days of British glam rock in the early 1970s, when dressing up and flamboyant styles were not only permitted but encouraged. "They longed for the days of British glam rock in the early 1970s when it was okay to dress up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Tribes of Alt-Rock

podcast.title: New York Dolls' Extension of Style
podcast.body: The New York Dolls significantly extended the glam rock aesthetic, pushing the look "miles further" with their makeup, spandex, and fishnets, creating a highly shocking and provocative image in Manhattan. "And yeah, people had heard about this glam rock thing that was happening in London, but it was nothing like this. The dolls took that look miles further."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 2

podcast.title: Origin and Aesthetics
podcast.body: Glam Rock began with Mark Bolan of T-Rex appearing on "Top of the Pops" in March 1971, wearing satin clothes covered with glitter dust, which David Bowie found brilliant. Bowie, inspired by Bolan, Iggy Pop, Lou Reed, and The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, fully embraced the genre by using his acting and mime lessons, experimenting with makeup and costuming, and adopting a revolutionary haircut. "This was the beginning of Glam Rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Why Bowie Still Matters - Part 1

podcast.title: Origin and Pioneers
podcast.body: Glam music was not pioneered by David Bowie, who was merely its greatest exponent in the 1970s white movement. Instead, Marc Bolan of T-Rex is identified as the person who perfectly connected the late 1960s psychedelic era with the 1970s glam movement, making him arguably the genre's true originator. "David Bowie no fue el pionero de la música glam, él no fue esa primera persona, no fue la persona que conecta la música del reino nido que había en el reino nido a finales de los años 60, con lo que fue el movimiento de la música glam de los años 70."

srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: Origins and Bowie's Embrace
podcast.body: Glam rock emerged in March 1971, notably influenced by Marc Bolan's appearance on "Top of the Pops" wearing satin clothes and glitter dust. David Bowie, inspired by this and other artists like Iggy Pop, Lou Reed, and The Legendary Stardust Cowboy, decided to "go all in" on the genre, creating the Ziggy Stardust persona. "It was the beginning of glam rock and he wanted a piece of it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Remembering David Bowie: Part 1

podcast.title: Peak and Widespread Influence
podcast.body: Glam rock reached its peak around 1974, extending its influence beyond punk and post-punk into various rock acts. Artists like Elton John, Queen (with Freddie Mercury's flamboyance), and Kiss (with their makeup) visibly adopted glam aesthetics. Richard O'Brien, author of *The Rocky Horror Picture Show*, reportedly listened exclusively to glam rock during its creation. Even The Rolling Stones and Rod Stewart embraced glam trappings in the mid-1970s. "Glam peaks sometime around 1974... Glam seeped into other areas of rock beyond just punk and all the other post-punk genres."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

podcast.title: Performance and Aesthetic
podcast.body: A defining characteristic of glam was the artists' stage behavior, which constituted "almost 90% of the show." This included eccentric, irreverent, explicit, and provocative conduct, coupled with an androgynous, colorful, often leopard-print aesthetic. Lyrics typically shifted from intellectual themes to more loving, sexually explicit, romantic, and melancholic ballads. "el comportamiento de los artistas en el escenario era casi el 90% del espectáculo."

srcs.episode: EL PIONERO DEL GLAM: MARC BOLAN Y T REX

podcast.title: Social and Sexual Commentary
podcast.body: Emerging barely post-Stonewall, glam rock challenged traditional notions of masculinity within rock music, creating a gender-bending brand of rock and roll. While not all glam stars were gay, the movement made space for non-heterosexual identities and reflected a societal sexual identity crisis. "Rock music was and is the domain of masculinity but glam rock challenged what that even means."

srcs.episode: Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s
Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s

podcast.title: Societal Mirror and Safe Space
podcast.body: Glam rock is seen as a mirror of society, reflecting and creating a safe space for changing viewpoints on gender and sexual identity. The theatrical packaging, though sometimes criticized as inauthentic, was compared to the rhinestone Nudie suits of male country artists, suggesting that authenticity is a personal relationship between the listener and the music. "If popular music really is a mirror of society As I believe it is Then Glam was not only a method of expressing Some of our changing viewpoints It created this safe space for it."

srcs.episode: Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s
Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s

podcast.title: Swadeheds' Musical Interest
podcast.body: Swadeheds, a British subculture, also appreciated British glam rock, surprisingly aligning with the musical preferences of their Teddyboy rivals. "As for music, Swades like British glam, just like their Teddyboy rivals, but they also shared a skinhead interest in soul, reggae, and sky."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Tribes of Alt-Rock

podcast.title: Transition to Hair Metal
podcast.body: By the late 1970s, glam rock began evolving into 80s hair metal, demonstrating that like many 70s genres, it did not die but was "reborn as something else." "By the late 70s Glam is on its way to becoming 80s hair metal."

srcs.episode: Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s
Ep. 26 - Starmen - Glam Rock of the 70s

podcast.title: Transition to Metal
podcast.body: The song "Love is Like Oxygen" by Sweet is cited as an example of the transition of glam rock into metal, indicating a stylistic evolution within the band's career and the genre itself. "Love is like oxygen shows the transition of glam rock to metal."

podcast.title: UK Dominance, US Influence
podcast.body: Glam Rock dominated the UK charts in the first half of the 1970s, making "smaller ripples in America" but proving "very influential" in setting the stage for the next British invasion. "Glam Rock, which dominated the UK charts in the first half of the decade, made smaller ripples in America but proved very influential."
